hook.text: Skin that senses temperature, pressure, and humidity — e-skin wraps sensors in flexible, stretchable biocompatible materials.

buildup.text: Thin-film transistors on polymer substrates create arrays of pressure sensors — matching the sensitivity of human fingertips.

discovery.text: Self-healing e-skin repairs cuts using dynamic polymer bonds — the material reconnects like biological tissue after damage.

twist.text: Powering e-skin is hard — flexible form limits battery options, but triboelectric generators harvest motion energy.

climax.text: E-skin on prosthetic hands gives amputees a sense of touch — pressure signals route through nerve interfaces to the brain.

punchline.text: Feel with electronics — e-skin restores sensation where biology cannot.

quiz.question: How does self-healing electronic skin repair itself?
options: Embedded batteries melt and reseal the damaged area
Dynamic polymer bonds reform after cuts, reconnecting the material like biological tissue healing
A layer of liquid adhesive flows over the damaged region

details.summary: Electronic skin combines flexible electronics with biological materials to create wearable sensors that monitor health metrics continuously. These ultra-thin patches measure heart rate, blood glucose, sweat chemistry, and muscle activity, transmitting data wirelessly to medical systems.
details.whyItMatters: Continuous health monitoring without bulky devices enables earlier disease detection and real-time clinical feedback. Electronic skin bridges the gap between medical devices and everyday wearables, making preventive healthcare seamlessly integrated
takeaways: Electronic skin uses flexible materials thinner than a bandage for health monitoring
Sensors can measure glucose, electrolytes, and cortisol from sweat continuously
Wireless data transmission enables real-time clinical monitoring remotely

faq.question: How thin and flexible can electronic skin be?
faq.answer: State-of-the-art electronic skin patches are under 100 micrometers thick, thinner than a human hair. They conform to skin wrinkles and stretch with movement without cracking. Some versions adhere with van der Waals forces alone, requiring no adhesive tape.

faq.question: Can electronic skin replace blood tests for glucose monitoring?
faq.answer: Sweat-based glucose sensors correlate with blood glucose levels but with a time lag and lower precision. They are improving rapidly with microfluidic sweat sampling and calibration algorithms. For diabetic management, they may supplement but not fully replace blood monitoring yet.
